question:
A 47-year-old woman with a medical history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and trigeminal neuralgia
presents for a routine check-up. She reports ongoing fatigue, difficulty sleeping, and knee pain, all of
which are chronic issues. She denies any recent infections. Her facial pain has improved significantly
since starting carbamazepine 6 weeks ago, as prescribed by her neurologist, but her energy levels
remain low. Her current medications include carbamazepine, acetaminophen, metformin, lisinopril, and
hydrochlorothiazide. She consumes alcohol about twice per week, averaging one drink per occasion.
Physical examination reveals no abnormalities. Laboratory results show a leukocyte count of 3200/mm³
(reference range: 4500–11,000/mm³), with an absolute neutrophil count of 1400/mm³ (reference range:
1900–7600/mm³) and a normal differential. Hemoglobin is 16.0 g/dL (reference range: 12.0–16.0 g/dL),
and platelet count is 327,000/mm³ (reference range: 150,000–350,000/mm³). Peripheral blood smear
findings are unremarkable. Her medical records indicate that her leukocyte counts over the past
decade have typically ranged between 5000 and 9000/mm³. What is the most appropriate next step in
the evaluation of this patient’s leukopenia? Answer Choices: (A) Evaluation for splenomegaly through
abdominal ultrasound (B) Initiation of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor therapy (C) Testing for
autoimmune markers such as antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor (D) Bone marrow aspiration
and biopsy (E) Referral to a hematologist for further evaluation (F) Ongoing observation with serial
hematologic surveillance (G) Testing for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria with flow cytometry (H)
Sequential discontinuation of medications, beginning with carbamazepine, and monitoring for
improvement (I) Genetic testing for inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (J) Testing for HIV,
hepatitis B and C viruses, vitamin B12, folic acid, and copper
 A. Sequential discontinuation of medications, beginning with carbamazepine, and monitoring for
improvement
B. Ongoing observation with serial hematologic surveillance
C. Referral to a hematologist for further evaluation
D. Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy
E. Testing for autoimmune markers such as antinuclear antibodies and rheumatoid factor
F. Testing for HIV, hepatitis B and C viruses, vitamin B12, folic acid, and copper
G. Genetic testing for inherited bone marrow failure syndromes
H. Testing for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria with flow cytometry
I. Initiation of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor therapy
J. Evaluation for splenomegaly through abdominal ultrasound
